title: Block’s new voice model sounds eerily human
content:
Jack Dorsey’s Block released a new voice model out of the company’s research lab that runs locally and sounds strangely human with its expressions like laughs, pauses, and cries. The company said the model, called Dessa, is trained fully on human speech and a single NVIDIA GPU rack.
Dessa is a full-duplex model, which means it can talk and listen at the same time, just like the GPT-Live model OpenAI released earlier this year. Typically, speech models are paired with a large language model for knowledge retrieval. Block said that Dessa’s knowledge stems from the conversational data it has.
Block said that the current models can sound unnatural and annoying because they have text in the pipeline that drives speech generation. A lot of models like ElevenLabs v4 or Fish Audio Drama 3 use voice tags to drive emotion in speech generation. Dorsey’s company claims that emotion is built into its model. It’s not clear if that emotion is being steered by some kind of tags.
“Interacting with current voice AI can just plain suck. It turns your voice into text and throws away an incredible amount of information text alone can’t carry. The most powerful AIs in the world can’t hear how you feel. We think that’s ridiculous, leads to a worse experience, and is potentially dangerous,” the company said in a blog post.
The company’s researchers posted multiple examples of conversations with Dessa where the agent had different voices, cadences, and emotions. For instance, in the conversation, the bot said it was tired from work, and at that point it sounded tired.
In the example below, the bot was talking about the person making it comfortable while sounding emotional and almost breaking down.
Another one shows a Block team member playing a game with the voice assistant.
The company said that the model can run locally on a consumer-grade computer such as a MacBook M4 Max or better. However, there is no public access to Dessa at the moment, and Block has put out a call for safety researchers to test the model. This is likely to test out cases where a voice agent could trick people on the other end.
Block is in the business of finance and selling its solutions to small businesses. Square already uses voice AI to handle ordering. But with its own voice model that can run on-device, it can power a lot more business and consumer experiences at a lower cost.

report.summary: Block’s research lab released Dessa, a local full-duplex voice model that expresses human-like emotion and is being opened to safety researchers for testing.
report.background: Voice AI has largely relied on a cascade: speech recognition turns audio into text, a large language model generates a reply, and text-to-speech renders it. That pipeline can add latency and strip out tone, pauses, laughter and other paralinguistic cues. Recent products such as OpenAI’s GPT-Live have pushed toward full-duplex conversation, while systems like ElevenLabs and Fish Audio use voice tags to steer emotion. Block, known for Square and fintech tools for small businesses, is betting that an end-to-end model trained on human speech can preserve emotional context and run locally. The company also has commercial incentives: voice ordering and customer service could become cheaper and more natural if inference happens on-device rather than through cloud APIs.
key_points: Dessa is a full-duplex model, meaning it can listen and speak at the same time. Block says it was trained entirely on human speech using a single NVIDIA GPU rack, and it can run locally on consumer hardware such as a MacBook M4 Max or better.

Block argues that conventional voice AI sounds unnatural because text sits in the pipeline. It claims Dessa has emotion built in rather than relying on voice tags, though it is unclear whether tags or other controls still steer expressions. The company says current voice AI can lose how users feel.

Demo conversations show Dessa shifting voice, cadence and emotion. In one example, the agent says it is tired from work and sounds tired; in another it sounds emotional and nearly breaks down. A Block team member also plays a game with the assistant, highlighting interactive use.

Dessa is not publicly available. Block has issued a call for safety researchers to test it, likely to probe misuse cases where a voice agent could deceive people on the other end of a call. That safety-first rollout contrasts with a broad consumer launch.

The model fits Block’s business. Square already uses voice AI for ordering, and an on-device model could power more business and consumer experiences at lower cost. Block sells finance and business tools, so natural voice interfaces could become a differentiator for small merchants.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Dessa reinforces the move from cascaded speech pipelines to end-to-end, full-duplex voice models that preserve tone and timing. If Block’s claims hold, emotional expression stops being a tag layer and becomes part of the model’s training objective. For developers, local inference on a MacBook-class machine could reduce cloud costs and latency and improve privacy, but limited access means most teams cannot build on it yet. For regular users, the upside is more natural, responsive voice agents; the risk is that human-sounding agents become harder to distinguish from people, raising deception and consent concerns. Block’s safety testing is a recognition that realism cuts both ways.
report.tools: Dessa is not public, so follow Block’s research releases and safety-researcher program. For comparison, watch OpenAI’s GPT-Live for full-duplex conversation, ElevenLabs v4 and Fish Audio Drama 3 for expressive voice tags, and Kyutai’s Moshi as an open-source full-duplex speech project. Developers building voice agents can also explore open frameworks such as Pipecat and LiveKit Agents for orchestration, though they rely on separate speech and language models.
